stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Paleobotanist Ines Carvalho reconstructs ancient forests from the fossil pollen preserved in lake sediments. Her 2021 analysis of a core drilled in northern Portugal, a column of mud recording roughly 40,000 years______ showed that oak woodland returned to the region nearly two thousand years earlier than previous studies had estimated.
explanation: The comma after "Portugal" opens a description of the core: "a column of mud recording roughly 40,000 years." A comma opened it, so a comma has to close it. Cross the phrase out and you get "Her 2021 analysis of a core drilled in northern Portugal showed that...", which is a complete sentence. The closing comma after "years" is the only thing still needed.

A.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("Her 2021 analysis") and its verb ("showed"). A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and neither side is one here.

B.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "Portugal" started the description, and without a matching comma after "years" it never ends, so it runs straight into the main verb.

D.why: Adding "and" makes "showed" look like the second of two joined verbs. The sentence has no first verb for it to pair with, so the main clause falls apart.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Agronomists at an experimental farm in central Iowa have spent a decade testing cover crops, which are plants grown between cash-crop seasons to protect the soil. The team's best performer—cereal rye sown in late October and left standing until the following spring______ reduced the nitrate washing out of the test plots by nearly a third.
explanation: The dash after "performer" opens an interruption that names the crop and describes how it was grown. An interruption opened with a dash has to close with a dash. Remove the interruption and you get "The team's best performer reduced the nitrate...", which is a complete sentence.

B.why: You closed the interruption with a different mark from the one that opened it. A dash cannot be paired with a comma; the two ends have to match.

C.why: You left the interruption open. Without a closing dash, "spring" runs straight into "reduced," and the reader cannot tell where the extra information ends.

D.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("The team's best performer") and its verb ("reduced"). Neither side is a complete sentence, so a semicolon cannot go here.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When inspectors examined the Harlow Creek Bridge in 2019, they found that its original steel bearings had rusted in place, leaving the deck unable to shift. The replacements, rubber-and-steel pads that allow the deck to ______ were installed over a single weekend without closing the bridge to traffic.
choices: expand, and contract, as temperatures change,
expand and contract as temperatures change
expand and contract as temperatures change;
expand and contract as temperatures change,
explanation: The comma after "replacements" opens a description of the pads, and that description ends at "change." Close it with a comma there and add nothing inside it. "Expand and contract" is one compound verb, and "as temperatures change" tells you when that happens, so no commas belong between them. Take the description out and "The replacements were installed..." is a complete sentence.

A.why: You scattered commas inside the description. "Expand and contract" is a single pair of verbs, and fencing off "and contract" breaks it up for no reason.

B.why: You left the description open. The comma after "replacements" needs a partner after "change"; without it, the phrase runs straight into "were installed."

C.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("The replacements") and its verb ("were installed"). What comes before the semicolon is not a complete sentence.

stimulus: In 2016, planners in the city of Aldren closed a nine-block section of downtown to through traffic, a move that local merchants initially opposed. The plan's most visible feature, a chain of shaded plazas built on what had once been four-lane intersections______ now draws more pedestrians on an average weekday than any other part of the city.
explanation: The comma after "feature" opens an appositive describing the plazas. It opened with a comma, so it closes with a comma after "intersections." Take it out and you get "The plan's most visible feature now draws more pedestrians...", which is grammatical.

A.why: You closed a comma-opened appositive with a dash. The marks around an interruption must match, so a comma needs a comma.

C.why: You left the appositive open. Without a closing comma, "intersections" reads as if it were the subject of "draws," and the main clause gets lost.

D.why: Adding "and" suggests two things are being joined, but "draws" is the sentence's only main verb. With "and" in front of it, the subject never gets a verb of its own.

explanation: The comma after "responsible" opens an appositive, and that appositive contains its own clause ("that orbits closer... than Mercury does to the Sun"). The whole appositive ends at "Sun," and because it opened with a comma, it closes with one. Remove it and "The object responsible is among the largest planets..." is a complete sentence.

B.why: You left the appositive open. The clause inside it made you lose track of the opening comma, and without a closing comma the phrase runs straight into "is."

C.why: You closed a comma-opened appositive with a dash. Punctuation around an interruption has to match at both ends.

D.why: You put a semicolon between the subject ("The object responsible") and its verb ("is"). The words before it cannot stand alone as a sentence.

explanation: The dash after "dams" opens an interruption describing how large the ponds became. A dash opened it, so a dash must close it after "years." Take the interruption out and "The ponds behind the dams soon supported twice as many dragonfly species..." is a complete sentence.

A.why: Adding "and" makes "supported" look like a second verb joined to the first. But "grew" belongs inside the interruption, so "The ponds" is left without a main verb of its own.

B.why: You left the interruption open. Without a closing dash, the description runs straight into "soon supported," and you cannot tell where the main sentence picks up again.

D.why: You closed the interruption with a comma even though a dash opened it. The two ends of an interruption must use the same mark.
